deep.reconstruction:
This page is the continuation of §2 ('Vergleichung der rationalen Zahlen mit den Punkten einer geraden Linie') and the opening of §3 ('Stetigkeit der geraden Linie') of an early draft of what became Dedekind's 'Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen' (1872).

(1) Embedding of Q into the line L. The previous page fixed an origin o and a unit length E. For positive integers m, n, lay off the segment E/n m times from o to the right or to the left. The resulting endpoints are taken to be the points p(+m/n) and p(-m/n), and p(0) = o. In modern terms there is a map p: Q -> L, p(r) = o + r·E, with the sign giving the direction.

Dedekind asserts two things. First, each rational corresponds to one and only one point. Second, the map preserves order and betweenness: if a > b then p(a) lies to the right of p(b); and if b lies between a and c, then p(b) lies between p(a) and p(c).

Implicit and not stated (my filling): p must be well defined, i.e. km/kn must give the same point as m/n. This holds because (E/kn)·km = (E/n)·m. Also implicit: injectivity follows from strict order preservation.

(2) Start of §3. A line drawn from the centred heading '§3. Stetigkeit der geraden Linie' to the paragraph 'Von der größten Wichtigkeit ...' shows that §3 begins there. The key remark is that there are points, indeed infinitely many, corresponding to no rational number.

The argument runs as follows:
- If α = p(a) with a rational, then the length oα is commensurable with the unit E. That is, there is a third segment (a common measure, 'gemeinschaftliches Maaß') of which both are integer multiples. Indeed, if a = m/n, then E/n is a common measure, with oα = m·(E/n) and E = n·(E/n).
- But, as is known since antiquity (the draft says 'Plato ....', presumably a placeholder for the Theaetetus reference), there are infinitely many lengths incommensurable with E. An example is the diagonal of the square on E, of length sqrt(2)·E.
- Laying off such a length from o gives an endpoint that is p(r) for no rational r. This conclusion is completed on the next page, which infers that the line is 'unendlich viel vollständiger' in point-individuals than Q is in number-individuals.

Logically this is the contrapositive: p(r) implies commensurability, and incommensurability implies the point is not in p(Q). The infinitude of such lengths is asserted, not proved. It follows easily, e.g. from q·sqrt(2) for rational q ≠ 0, or sqrt(2) + q.
errors: Well-definedness of p(m/n) under change of representative (km/kn) is left implicit.

The claim that infinitely many incommensurable lengths exist is cited as known ('bekanntlich', 'Plato ....' left as placeholder) rather than proved. The incommensurability of the diagonal is likewise only cited. This is acceptable for an expository draft.
The order/betweenness preservation is asserted without proof. It is routine: p(a) - p(b) = (a - b)E.

results.what: Order-preserving injection of the rationals into a directed line with origin and unit (number line), preserving betweenness
results.modern_name: Embedding of the ordered field Q into the real line / number line
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Descartes, Wallis, etc.); this exact exposition is Dedekind, Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen (1872), §2

results.what: Existence of (infinitely many) points of the line not corresponding to any rational number, via incommensurability of the square's diagonal with its side
results.modern_name: Irrationality of sqrt(2); incompleteness of Q relative to the line
results.usually_credited_to: Pythagoreans / Theodorus–Theaetetus (as reported by Plato); Euclid Book X. Its use as motivation for continuity is Dedekind 1872, §3

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of §§2–3 of Dedekind's published 'Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen' (1872), matching the published text nearly verbatim. The only unpublished details are minor: an explicit 'Plato ....' placeholder reference that is absent from the print, and the placement of the §3 heading. The mathematics is classical.

checkable.asserts: The diagonal of the unit square, length sqrt(2), is incommensurable with the unit (irrational).
The diagonal of the square with unit side has length sqrt(2) (Pythagoras).

Sample instances of infinitely many incommensurable lengths (q*sqrt(2), sqrt(2)+q for rational q ≠ 0).

transcription_corrections: The heading '§ 3. Stetigkeit der geraden Linie.' is not at the end of the page. It is written in the middle column, with a connecting line drawn to the paragraph beginning 'Von der größten Wichtigkeit ist nun aber die Bemerkung ...'. §3 therefore begins at that paragraph, consistent with the published 1872 text, where §3 opens 'Von der größten Wichtigkeit ist nun aber die Tatsache ...'.
The words 'keiner', 'commensurabel mit der Längeneinheit' and 'incommensurabel' are underlined in the manuscript.
The struck word after 'daß es' is plausibly 'unendlich' but is hard to read; the reading is uncertain.
The letters visible at the right margin belong to the facing folio (the next page) and are not part of this page's text.
